items.question: How do you see verification shaping progress in AI for Science?
items.object: Verification in AI for Science
items.answer: For AI for Science, I think verification is definitely the hardest part. It is a bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is broken, you can iterate very quickly. Mathematics has moved from an era in which proofs were scarce into an era of proof oversupply.

items.question: How do you judge the meaning of AI discoveries that humans cannot understand?
items.object: AI discoveries that humans cannot understand
items.answer: I think they can only have partial meaning. A result being correct does not necessarily mean it is truly correct. You need to understand it and then evaluate it. If we acknowledge and accept this AI as a black box, and comfortably accept the results it produces, that will create many difficulties. If a result is not fully explainable, then the process of abstracting concepts may, I think, be AGI’s final last mile. If AI wants to win a Nobel Prize, it will take a long time.

items.question: How do you assess the pressures Google and DeepMind have faced around Gemini?
items.object: Google and DeepMind’s organizational and competitive challenges around Gemini
items.answer: I think this should be interpreted from several angles. First, Google and DeepMind have many talented people and many teams. Perhaps a few years ago, each team focused on its own topics and did not interfere much with one another. But starting three or four years ago, with the Gemini project—because Gemini is, after all, the biggest and a very important project—such a project requires concentrating resources to accomplish a major task. From that point onward, this created major challenges for the management of the overall personnel organization and projects. So some internal conflicts were inevitable. The second background factor is that, I believe everyone can see that Gemini’s performance over roughly the past half year has been less than satisfactory. At the beginning of this year, Gemini 3.1 Pro could perhaps still be considered a relatively good language model on the rankings. But over the past three or four months, people have seen the capabilities of models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and many Chinese open-source companies advance by leaps and bounds. By comparison, Gemini 3.5 Flash and the newest 3.6 Flash have performed rather ordinarily. Everyone is also eagerly awaiting a 3.x Pro, which has not yet been formally released. Overall, Gemini is very far behind on progress. Under such circumstances, it is also very difficult to catch up commercially—for example, by shifting the business model toward emerging capabilities centered on coding agents, as Anthropic has done.

items.question: Why do you see Discovery Loop’s focus on automated scientific research as a natural next step for AI?
items.object: Discovery Loop and the emergence of AI for scientific knowledge discovery
items.answer: The subject matter of Discovery Loop, founded by Jeff Dean, Oriol, Sanjay, and Quoc, is itself about enabling AI to conduct knowledge development, knowledge discovery, and automated scientific research. This is highly aligned with the direction our startup wanted to pursue. I mean, there is a certain logical, very natural extension here, because AI has now reached this stage of development. Over the past two or three years, mathematics and programming have been among the clearest demonstrations of AI’s intelligence, and probably what people have focused on most: automatically writing code and solving Olympiad mathematics problems. Naturally, once those problems are addressed, one can imagine what the next topic will be that allows AI intelligence to explode, generate enormous benefits, or help humanity solve bigger problems. Clearly, it is extending capabilities in mathematics and code to broader scientific knowledge discovery. So, starting this year, you can see many startups around knowledge discovery, AI for Science, and recursive self-improvement. I believe that if a star team like Jeff, Oriol, Sanjay, and Quoc goes out to create a startup, it must want to set a new benchmark in this field and become a new kind of lab, a new Neolab.

items.question: How do you evaluate the claim that Jeff Dean and other prominent leaders leaving to start Discovery Loop marks the end of Google’s era in AI?
items.object: Google’s AI prospects following the departure of prominent leaders
items.answer: Saying that a new era has begun and Google has turned away or something like that—I think that is overstating it. Google possesses every ingredient needed to make language models well. It is not that the company cannot continue just because one or two people—even leaders such as these—change roles, right? Of the major technology companies, Google is perhaps the company with all the full-stack elements for doing AI well: from underlying chips, infrastructure, and data centers, to tooling, the model layer, talent, and data, and then product distribution above that and the whole product stack, with broad distribution channels for consumer products. It has all of them and does not rely at all on an external ecosystem. So it is not that Google cannot do it well; rather, it needs some adjustments in priorities and resource investment. But I believe Google will still build this capability up in the future.

items.question: What motivated you to leave Google to pursue AI for scientific discovery?
items.object: Cao Yuan’s motivation for leaving Google to pursue AI for scientific discovery
items.answer: First, I want to say that in the Bay Area, in Silicon Valley, personnel movement among these few frontier technology companies is currently very frequent. It is not just Google. Personally, the reason I was able to think of doing something like this is that we were previously also working on Gemini, constantly iterating models and doing post-training. But I had always been thinking about deeper questions: intelligence, and how to make these models more intelligent. If you want to achieve the AGI goal, current models can indeed do mathematics and write code, but some capabilities are clearly still missing. For example, if you really want them to handle scientific problems and solve scientific problems, their capacity for innovation—their ability to propose new hypotheses, verify new hypotheses, and continuously update themselves—is still far from being able to help people increase scientific knowledge exponentially. So why is that capability missing, right? And how can we further improve the model so that it can help humanity do better things? That was one of my motivations for deciding to come out and give it a try.

So he is indeed a very legendary figure. And the other colleagues who left with him—Oriol and Quoc were both early members of Google Brain and have worked together for a long time. items.question: How do you understand Google DeepMind’s difficulty retaining scientists pursuing AI for Science?
items.object: Google DeepMind’s research priorities and management challenges amid scientist departures
items.answer: Inside Google now, DeepMind’s highest priority must be to make Gemini good—to reach SOTA, to be on par with Anthropic and OpenAI, or better. Therefore, in the short term, much of the work focus and priorities must shift in that direction. This includes Jumper and people who originally worked on AI4S; their work focus will also change. In such a large team, with such a high-priority project, you cannot make every individual fully satisfied. Google has so many talented people, and everyone wants to do their own work and has their own ideas. So how to enable all these people’s capabilities and aspirations to be expressed to the fullest, and how to make the best arrangements, is very challenging. I think Google has in fact already done a great deal of optimization and adjustment in this regard, so that each person can realize their greatest potential. Certainly, throughout this process, the management team, scientists, and engineers are all thinking about and continually updating and iterating the process. There are many management challenges, but I believe the situation is improving.

items.question: How do you distinguish AI for Science, AI for AI, and Recursive Self-Improvement?
items.object: AI for Science, AI for AI, and Recursive Self-Improvement
items.answer: AI4S and AI4AI both treat the AI model itself as a researcher, to study scientific problems or problems concerning AI itself. Think about AI for AI: my model is already very intelligent—so how can I leverage the model’s intelligence to improve some of its own capabilities? For example, if you give it a requirement, a task: can you train this model as well as possible using the fewest resources and fewest GPUs, within a fixed budget? Of course people can do this, but if AI can do it itself, it may be much faster than people at trying many new ideas and experiments. For instance, it may look at your current model codebase and find that a parameter could be set higher. It will generate a proposal, a recommendation: first try raising this parameter. Because AI’s agent capabilities are already very strong, it can write some code to implement the proposal, automatically put it in a sandbox to run the experiment and train the model, and then observe the final results, its training results. After obtaining that result, it treats it as feedback—and proposes the next step: I found that after you raised this parameter slightly, the model improved. Should I continue moving in this direction? Based on such feedback, it further generates its next recommendation. After round after round of iteration, you can see the model’s performance continually improving step by step. This is a process of continual self-regression. So that is a very simple application of AI4AI. Of course, people are now using AI for AI. Some startups are exploring whether they can find architectures different from Transformers, because that may require extensive search and many new ideas. Others are exploring whether AI4AI can find a new optimization algorithm that does not require Backpropagation—backward gradient propagation. So if AI is used to study problems, it can search many different methods more efficiently, try many methods, and complete the entire loop itself. Similarly, AI for Science simply changes the problem: you use AI to address scientific problems, but the overall approach is similar. RSI is not a task; it is a method. As I described earlier, it is the ability to continuously self-iterate: Recursive Self-Improvement. You keep using self-iteration to update the task or update the proposal, so that it can continuously make itself better at the task. So that is the distinction among these concepts. AI4S and AI4AI are actually similar; only their objectives differ. RSI is a method that can be used for AI for AI or AI4S.

items.question: Why do you think AI for Science is ready to take off now?
items.object: The technological conditions enabling AI for Science to take off
items.answer: I think AI’s development in the past two years has been most clearly demonstrated in reasoning and intelligence by code and mathematics. Once these two are in place—once AI can reliably write code—and once the AI agent and its entire harness, meaning the external setup that helps the AI complete a workflow step by step, have matured, you can make the AI address more complex scientific problems. For example, if you want to run a biological experiment, first the model needs to propose a hypothesis: what experiment should be run next? That requires reasoning, deriving the next step from current experimental observations. That is the first step. Second, once the experiment produces a result and you receive the data, it needs to write code to analyze whether the data match the expectation. That is the second step, and it requires strong coding ability. Third, after generating the code, how does it update itself? If the analysis finds anomalies in the data, it needs to analyze, step by step, why the data are anomalous and whether there was a problem with its earlier proposal, continually self-iterating. So all of this requires the model’s own reasoning capability, data-analysis capability, mathematics and coding capability, and the overall agent loop—the full loop capability. This includes memory management: after each run, it has memories, and you must put the previous observations into a memory-management container. Once these capabilities are in place, you can better tackle science problems, because science spans a very broad area and its problems are very complex—perhaps more challenging than coding and math. So now the timing, geography, and people are all aligned; it is time to use AI for Science.

items.question: How do you judge which scientific fields are most attractive for AI for Science?
items.object: The relative appeal of scientific fields for AI for Science
items.answer:
I think the appeal is determined by several factors: market potential, market size, whether it is suitable for AI, where there is urgency for AI-driven science R&D, and whether it can be done well.

Traditionally, biology, biotech, life science, or drug discovery have large markets. This has nothing to do with AI; they have always been large markets. Even without AI, the market itself is large. That is the first point. The second is that in biology and pharmaceuticals, the overall process is comparatively standardized and already fairly structured, and the data are abundant. The whole process is relatively easy for AI to handle.

The third is that for pharmaceutical companies, especially those developing new drugs, the cycle is extremely long and the costs are very high. For example, to develop a new drug, you need to test many, many possible new molecular structures and select some leads—the most promising ones. That is only the first part. After that, for some relatively reliable molecular structures, you still need clinical trials and further drug development, as well as many regulatory processes. The entire cycle may cost hundreds of millions of U.S. dollars, and by the time it is ultimately approved, several years may have passed. How AI can automate this process or reduce costs is therefore a very appealing topic for pharma and drug manufacturers. Overall, biology and drug development are certainly relatively large areas for venture investment and attractive scientific topics for applying AI.

Materials also have a large market; materials arise in every aspect of life. But compared with drugs, the materials market is very fragmented, and it is hard to say where to capture the value. You may have metal materials, leather materials, biomaterials, materials used in semiconductor manufacturing, rare-earth materials, and so on. The segmentation is very fine, and the whole development process also differs by application. So although it is a large market, the market is too fragmented for you to handle it with one relatively standardized method.

And even if you invent a new material—discover a new material structure or a new material molecule—that is only the first step. Afterwards, for example, how do you use it in downstream production? Where is the invented material used? Who manufactures it? How is it ultimately packaged? Its value chain is relatively fragmented, and it is hard to capture all that value with AI at once. So this means materials are also a large market, but may be somewhat smaller relative to drug development and biology.

items.question: How do you distinguish the role of AI for Science in accelerating scientists’ work from its role in making discoveries?
items.object: AI for Science’s roles in accelerating research and generating discoveries
items.answer: I think that depends on the role of the AI for Science model. There are several roles. A workbench is like an IDE for programming, an integrated environment. It has many tools for analysis; you can converse with the model, which may give you suggestions or otherwise help you run experiments and simulations. It depends on the setting, the field, and whether your model is used in a specific vertical domain or as a general model within an agent loop. Its role is different.

items.question: How do you see AI’s role in defining scientific research problems?
items.object: Human and AI roles in defining scientific research problems
items.answer: I think humans must define the problem. I do not think AI can currently select an appropriate problem on its own with the requisite taste, then define an appropriate problem and conduct R&D on it. I think that is currently quite difficult: tailoring the problem. That is why human scientists remain indispensable. AI can do that, but its role there is mainly supportive. At present, people need to choose what kinds of problems are suitable for AI to study.

items.question: What makes a scientific problem suitable for AI in your view?
items.object: Scientific problems suitable for AI
items.answer: I think any problems that can be computed, and that are easy to verify and calculate, are most suited to AI. Put simply, it depends on how cleanly you can model the process. AlphaFold, for instance, has an extremely clear problem definition: given an amino-acid sequence, produce a tertiary structure. This kind of problem is highly structured, and AI can comparatively solve it through computation. Another factor is that the problem is relatively easy to verify. In all of AI for Science, perhaps the most difficult link is verification. AI4S is unlike AI for coding or math. With AI for coding and math, once mathematics provides a proof, or AI provides one, you can immediately judge whether it is correct. That is very fast. Or once you write code, you can immediately know whether it is correct. But for many scientific problems, if you apply for a new drug, you may not truly know how effective it is until after it reaches the market, even though there are many simulations. So the ultimate problem may not necessarily be solved quickly by AI4S. But certain steps within it may be suitable for AI: if simulations or simulation tools can calculate a drug’s properties, whether it is stable, or whether it may have side effects. Thus, how quickly AI can verify what it generates determines how quickly AI for Science can iterate. So verifiability is a very important metric.

items.question: How do you distinguish the roles and representation requirements of general models and specialized models in AI for Science?
items.object: General and specialized models in AI for Science
items.answer: First, I think we need to distinguish two concepts. At present, AI for Science mainly uses two kinds of models. One is a general model, such as GPT Codex and those GPT-family models. It drives the entire AI for Science reasoning process and analyzes data itself, and so on. That requires a very powerful general model. The second is a vertical-domain model itself, such as AlphaFold, materials models like GNoME or MatterGen, or models for weather forecasting. Such a model does only one domain; it is an expert in that domain but cannot do anything else. You cannot place it in a general orchestrator role—like a “lab director”—to drive the entire scientific-research process. Different models have different requirements for representation. A general model can represent anything. Like GPT or Gemini, you can give it a natural-language description as input, a piece of code, or JSON such as JSON-formatted laboratory data. But a model like AlphaFold is only for a specific domain, so it can accept only amino-acid sequences, along with some DNA or supplementary metadata—and therefore cannot perform reasoning beyond that domain. Indeed, the distinction—what a model can represent and what kinds of data it can receive—depends on its position in the overall platform. GPT-like models can serve as a large lab director, telling you what to do. Specialized models in particular domains, whether AlphaFold or GNoME, are experts; you can invoke them as tools.

items.question: How do you think an AI should decide which scientific experiment to pursue next?
items.object: AI selection of scientific experiments
items.answer: I see this as a search process. The AI model proposes different options, in the sense that it samples different plans at each step. You need a mechanism to decide which plan it should select next and test experimentally. You can imagine it as a tree. Each node on the tree is a plan that has been explored previously or is currently explored. You must decide which plan is most promising, then conduct experiments from that plan and push further downward. To do that, you need to assign each node a score. If one node is formulation one and another is formulation two, and the model finds that formulation one seems to have performed well according to prior experiments, then its score may be relatively higher in that respect. But it cannot focus entirely on formulation one, because the experiment is only halfway complete. You cannot push this path or plan all the way to the end based only on partial observations. So it needs an exploration process as well. For instance, it assigns some probability to formulation two and can consider formulation two. Thus, how important each node’s score is in deciding what to do next is a combination of the node’s current value and the probability that it has not yet been explored. Based on the final combined score, it can decide which plan is most worthwhile to develop next.

items.question: How do you think a closed loop from AI models to experimental verification can be built in AI for Science?
items.object: Closed loops in AI for Science
items.answer:
I think the closed loop is very important. Frankly, the reason Anthropic’s Claude coding agent has become arguably the most successful commercial closed-loop model, capable of generating exponential growth among AI applications, is that AI coding has this loop. A programmer writes a program, and it can immediately verify it and tell you whether it is correct. You do not need to wait or accept outside intervention; you can decide by yourself. As a user, this gives you a kind of trust in the coding agent. You can hand the entire task to it, and it is a process that you can fully verify.

But closed loops in AI for Science are difficult because they involve the physical world and require experiments. This is not as easy to verify as writing code. So, put simply, it is about how to obtain experimental data and experimental verification more quickly. Ideally, if you could obtain experimental verification once a minute, then the problem would be solved. I could generate countless data points and train directly on them. But that is not very feasible in most physical experimental environments.

One direction of development now is to make it an automated laboratory. If laboratory operating procedures are relatively standardized, you can replace them completely with robots. Many U.S. companies are doing this. If the process is not standardized—if formulations or the entire operation often need to change—you need embodied intelligence, a relatively general robot to do this. That may be a more distant prospect. But regardless, automated laboratories are certainly a relatively visible solution.

The second is how to reduce physical experiments as much as possible. If the bottleneck in the closed loop is physical experiments, and they are difficult or costly to conduct, you must make it perform as few experiments as possible, while ensuring each experiment is likely to have a good result and is set up correctly. This is what needs to improve in AI’s intelligence itself. items.question: How do you assess current language models’ ability to discover causal mechanisms in science?
items.object: Language models’ ability to discover causal mechanisms
items.answer: I think AI definitely can discover causal mechanisms. Causal modeling is actually a subject with a long history. Long ago, people such as Judea Pearl had already developed many causal models. But in the current AI4S context, discovering causal mechanisms means, put simply, enabling a language model to distinguish correlation from causation. I would say that is currently one of language models’ weaknesses. I cannot say definitively; my personal feeling is that they are not yet especially good at it. There are many studies and analyses where you give a language model a reasoning problem, and it infers the correct result, but if you slightly rephrase the premise or reverse the word order or sentence order while keeping the meaning unchanged, it may generate the wrong result. During training, language models generally see only one form of training example: how a correct description or the most common description should be stated. They have never seen how the same thing is described another way. So when you rephrase it in a way the model is unaccustomed to, it makes mistakes because it does not have that in its database. This happens often. That is why Yann LeCun and others emphasize building world models. You cannot have a language model trained only on surface-level text, because text reflects people’s most common ways of saying things or shows only positive examples; negative examples, stated in reverse, will not appear in text. If you can learn a world model and the internal laws of the physical world, that is independent of how you represent or describe something. If a world model can achieve that, its grasp of causal relationships may be far better than the current language model’s causal reasoning based on textual descriptions. Recently, some new startups have also been exploring efforts to train language models to capture causal relationships better. My personal feeling is that current language models can understand causal relationships in most cases when they are described in normal ways. But when something is unusual, or when you need interventions—what happens if I alter this variable, raise a certain value, or remove a condition, some so-called Do-Calculus—then in many cases they still cannot do it. They do not have a particularly complete process for understanding the physical world. Predicting correlation is what large language models can do now: X and Y are highly correlated. But science requires a highly definite, precise statement, such as: X causes Y through mechanism M. If representation relies only on language, it is difficult to establish that logical and causal relationship with great certainty.

items.question: What do you see as the fundamental problem with language models’ ability to reason about causal relationships?
items.object: The reliability of language models’ causal reasoning
items.answer: I think the issue is unreliability. It is not that it cannot do it. In many cases, language models can also handle causal relationships; otherwise, they could not complete many reasoning problems. But the issue is whether they are reliable. Whether they are reliable depends entirely on how you state the question, conclusion, or premise. If your phrasing is inconsistent with how things were phrased in its training data, or involves a new phenomenon it has not encountered, then the model is lost. It may not be able to extract the causal relationship. That is why a more fundamental level of judgment is needed. A model’s judgment of causal relationships should not be based on your linguistic phrasing; it should be based on its grasp of your entire physical model.

items.question: What do you see as the hardest technical challenge in AI for Science?
items.object: Technical bottlenecks in AI for Science
items.answer: I think the hardest part for AI for Science is definitely verification. It is in the physical world. Put it this way: verification may be the most important step. But if you get verification right, even using the simplest AI4S approach, it can solve many problems. As mentioned earlier, if you can obtain one data point per minute—obtain data from physical experiments—then ideally you can generate countless data points, and immediately re-post-train a model. Then, as with training for code or mathematics, the problem is solved. At least verification may be a very important link; it is a bottleneck. Once that bottleneck is broken, you can iterate very quickly. But that does not mean the problem is solved. The hardest part may be whether AI itself can put forward some new ideas—whether your model, no matter how it comes up with new proposals or how I perform reasoning, is forever limited to the knowledge currently available in papers. If it cannot put forward new hypotheses, or new ideas with more of a step-change quality, then in most cases, this loop is just continuously tuning parameters, continuously trying formulations, or doing permutations and combinations. The upper limit of what it can achieve is definitely limited; it is relatively low. So how can AI generate ideas that are more creative but also reasonable? I think this is an area that is still very inadequate at present. For example, some time ago Nobel laureate Jennifer Doudna—the person who works on gene editing—was interviewed. They asked her, “Do you use AI to help you conduct experiments or do scientific research?” She said, “We use it too, but among the proposals AI gives us, not one of its proposals is something we did not already know.” It generates many proposals, but none is something we did not know. There may be things we normally overlook, but fundamentally these are all already present in existing knowledge. We can already find them in papers or elsewhere. So whether it can propose plans that are both innovative and feasible is, I think, a very difficult problem.

items.question: Why do you think making a Nobel Prize-level scientific discovery remains so difficult for AI for Science?
items.object: AI for Science’s ability to make scientific discoveries
items.answer: Discovery is a highly challenging process. Current AI for Science may be able to recombine and search within its representation space, within existing concepts, and then design some new experimental plans or something similar. By recombining existing concepts, it can indeed solve some—one could say, a large portion of—problems. Its efficiency is already far higher than that of humans. But if you really want AI eventually to automatically generate a Nobel Prize-level scientific process, a scientific result, then this entire discovery process is something AI is still far from being able to do. First, you must receive perception—some sensory input. You observe people, conduct experiments, observe data. That is only the first step; it is the input of experience. But after the input, you must be able to form concepts. For example, you see someone push a cart, and the cart moves forward. That is a surface phenomenon you observe. Then you need to extract a concept: force, strength. He pushes, and the cart moves forward. You must also symbolize it, producing an F. Third, if you want to obtain a scientific theory, you need to crystallize and abstract it into a formula, like Newton’s second law, F = ma: force equals mass times a. In other words, you must abstract the most primitive observations into concepts, and finally formalize them into such a theoretical system. I think this entire discovery process is extremely difficult for AI. At present, it is still an extremely difficult matter for AI. So I think AI4S is currently only able, within certain limits and within an existing representation space, to carry out different explorations. It is not truly able to produce new theories or knowledge.

items.question: How do you understand symbolism’s strengths and limitations as an approach to artificial intelligence?
items.object: Symbolism as an approach to artificial intelligence
items.answer:
“Symbolism” is a concept that began very early in artificial intelligence, perhaps from the very beginnings of AI. It is a very broad concept, but simply put, it means writing rules. If some knowledge or phenomena can be stated very clearly, are a priori, and do not need to be described or learned through data, then you write them as symbols, formulas, or rules. For example, If-Then rules can be known without data. If you know A > B and B > C, then A > C. You can write such things in advance; you do not need to learn them.

That is the difference between symbolism and connectionism. Connectionism, bluntly speaking, is neural networks. Its representation is a distributed representation using a vector, so you need to learn it. With symbolism, I can simply write it by hand, express the knowledge using symbols. With connectionism, you have to learn it using vectors. Perhaps the meaning of each element is learned from the data you receive through observation.

The advantage of symbolism is that you can write something a priori, and it is very precise. Mathematics and code are in fact both symbolic. This may also include today’s Agent Harness: its entire workflow is specified a priori—what to do in the first step, what to do in the second, what to do if a particular situation arises, and when to call Memory. All of this is specified a priori. It definitely all belongs to symbolism. Because it is a priori, you can design it.

But its problem is that, as a method of knowledge representation, it is very brittle. For example, how do you express the concept of a cat? If you give me an image, how do I know whether it is a cat? Using symbols or rules, you might say: if an animal has two pointed ears, whiskers, and fur, then it is a cat. But this kind of representation is very brittle. You have no way to describe a cat purely in language. You cannot prescribe many things using one set of logic; you cannot characterize the entire universe with very rigid logic. In linguistic communication, many phenomena are very fuzzy. Change the photo of the cat—if the cat happens to be lowering its head, then it differs from the conditions you set in your logic. So it is very brittle. This is why symbolism did not become mainstream.

items.question: How do you see symbolic logic helping large language models generate new scientific ideas?

items.answer: We want to add a layer outside the LLM that can help it generate new ideas. items.question: What do you see as the main bottleneck in your approach combining large language models with symbolic reasoning to generate new ideas?
items.object: Balancing novelty and feasibility in AI-generated ideas
items.answer: I think it is balancing the novelty of its new ideas with feasibility. Honestly, making a model innovative is easy. Put plainly, when you propose a new idea, you need to prove that it actually fits your problem and is feasible, rather than being innovative merely for the sake of innovation.

items.question: How do you see symbolism’s future role alongside neural networks in AI?
items.object: The role of symbolism alongside connectionism in AI
items.answer: I would not call it a comeback, because many things we see in the world are indeed highly ambiguous. I do not think symbolism can necessarily make a comeback. I think it is unlikely to replace connectionism, because neural networks are ultimately extremely powerful. The language models everyone sees are all trained this way. But some things may be accelerated or strengthened by symbols. For example, in the end perhaps 98% is connectionism and 2% is symbolism. In fact, today’s AI for math and AI for coding are neuro-symbolic: structures that combine symbols and connectionism. For example, in solving mathematical problems, your original model first generates a mathematical proof; that may be a neural network, the connectionist part. But to determine whether the proof is correct, I need to use formal proof tools, languages such as Lean, to verify it. This entire set of tools is completely symbolic and has no relationship whatsoever with the neural network. So this is already an example of neural networks being connected with symbols. Both parts are important.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between today’s AI debates and classical philosophy’s accounts of human knowledge?
items.object: Classical philosophy as a framework for understanding AI and continual learning
items.answer: Whether it is symbols or connectionism, I think their essence is this: symbols are a priori; you can specify things without data. Connectionism—neural networks—requires you to learn things through a great deal of experience. I think this is related to many philosophical discussions throughout history. They are all discussions about how humans cognize the world. For example, the British empiricists, people like Francis Bacon and John Locke, believed that human cognition comes entirely from experience. My brain is blank: whatever kind of input you show me, my brain maps that input. My world is determined entirely by external sensory input and experiential material. In today’s AI context, that corresponds to large models. At the beginning, a model is random and has nothing in it, but after training on trillions of tokens, the model’s intelligence is determined entirely by those sensory and experiential inputs. That is completely an empiricist mapping in the contemporary context. On the other hand, rationalism holds that how people understand the world is entirely determined by certain innate structures of the brain. As Descartes said, “I think, therefore I am.” I first have a structure, and then I understand the world. How I understand the world is determined entirely without relying on experience or sensory input. These two schools, one a priori and one a posteriori, continued developing until Kant, who thought neither was right and wanted to unify them. Experience provides the material, but for sensory inputs to have meaning for you, you need an a priori structure. Otherwise, whether you see a sphere or a tire, it is merely a random input to you, and you cannot perceive the concept of roundness. So Kant believed that humans have a priori structures—roughly, he thought there were 12 categories—synthetic a priori judgments, structures such as those for time, space, objects, causality, and so on, that interpret the world and sensory experience. He believed that these two things must be combined in order to produce human intelligence and knowledge. Then later Hegel thought Kant was also wrong: you cannot set reason, sensibility, and experience in opposition; it is not a binary division. They should be dialectically unified. That is, you need to continuously update. You cannot say that once a concept is established—once the a priori is established—it remains fixed forever, right? So there must be continual self-negation and continual updating. Mapped into today’s context, into the context of AI products, that is continual learning. Once your model is trained, AGI ultimately cannot just be a file, a fixed checkpoint with all parameters carved into it, and call that intelligence. That certainly cannot be the case, right? It must continually recognize its own errors and update itself through ongoing interaction with users or while carrying out tasks, so that it can become more intelligent. Overall, what I mean is that whether it is symbolism or connectionism, these are concepts discussed in the AI context. But the topics they discuss are in fact part of the same lineage as classical philosophy. People in different periods consider problems from different perspectives, but they are all discussing the same question: how do humans come to know the world, and how is knowledge produced? Ancient scientists did not use computational language, but I think these inquiries are consistent.

items.question: How do you assess Google’s and OpenAI’s approaches to AI for Science?
items.object: Google’s and OpenAI’s investments in AI for Science
items.answer: I think it is clear that among these three companies, Google unquestionably made the earliest and broadest AI for Science investments. It could be said to be the company with the most research paths, and it had these efforts very early on. There is no doubt about that: the entire Alpha series, including recent efforts such as Co-Scientist and Gemini for Science. Anthropic and OpenAI of course recognize the importance of AI4S, so they have invested heavily in it. For example, OpenAI also started relatively early. When GPT-5 was released, it already had a white paper about using GPT-5 to solve all kinds of problems—mathematics, computer science, biology, and so on—and said it could already solve many scientific problems. It also has some very aggressive plans. For example, it publicly announced a goal of having an autonomous AI scientist by, it seems, 2027. It also has, as mentioned earlier, a closed-loop experiment involving OpenAI GPT and Ginkgo Bioworks’ AutoLab. This may be the most convincing closed-loop experiment so far, and the one with the best results. This is what OpenAI has done. items.question: How do you assess OpenAI’s strategy for investing in AI for Science?
items.object: OpenAI’s AI for Science strategy and priorities
items.answer: First, regarding OpenAI, I think it is being very aggressive in trying to catch up. But I think it may also have a problem in its AI4S deployment: its priorities. items.question: How do you think about the difficulty of using AI to solve mathematical problems?
items.object: The capabilities and bottlenecks of AI for mathematics
items.answer:
I do not think it is easy, but it depends on what kind of mathematics. Mathematics is a very broad concept. At present, there may be two relatively prominent AI-for-math startups: Axiom Math AI and Harmonic AI. Their methods may be broadly similar, and they are conducting some frontier explorations into how AI can do math better and how math can be commercialized—for example, work in verifiable domains, EDA, software design, or similar areas.

I think what problems AI for math can solve depends on the mathematical library, namely the Lean language and its mathematical library. To give a rough explanation: especially for more complex mathematics, you need the language model first to propose possible approaches to a proof. But the language model itself does not know whether the mathematical proof process is wrong. So what do you do? You have to automatically formalize the proof into a language called Lean. Once it compiles in Lean, the mathematical result must be correct. That proves that what the language model proposed is correct.

But there are several bottlenecks here. First, the language model itself needs to be strong enough to propose possible proof methods or new mathematical results. Second, there is the automated formalization process: how to convert a mathematical result described in natural language or mathematical notation into a language like Lean. This conversion, this translation process, is not particularly easy. This is also something companies like Axiom AI and Harmonic AI spend a lot of effort on. Third, if you want to solve more and harder mathematical problems, Lean itself needs a mathematical library, mathlib, that contains a great deal of relevant existing human mathematical knowledge. Those materials must already be there; otherwise it cannot assemble them. So this process also requires a lot of effort: how to put more of humanity’s existing mathematical knowledge into mathlib. These factors determine how far AI for math can go.

Lean is not necessary in every situation. But I think if you want to do mathematics seriously, properly, or at a professional mathematician’s level, you need Lean. For something like Olympiad competitions, the mathematics involved may not require a particularly large amount of knowledge or especially deep knowledge. They test whether a contestant has the creative ability to find a very complex construction or process. But the mathematical knowledge involved, including the proof process itself, may not be especially complicated. It may be only a page or two; it can certainly be written out. In that situation, if you train the language model well enough, its natural-language generation of the result can be credible to a considerable extent. And the IMO is, after all, just an exam: you submit the result quickly and can verify whether it is correct. As an exam setup, there is not much problem with that.

But imagine asking AI today to do something at Wang Hong’s level—a proof of more than 100 pages. If a language model generates more than 100 pages of mathematical proof entirely in natural language, it has no way to guarantee that it is correct. So if you want AI to do the work professional mathematicians do, to produce highly complex proofs, then to ensure the result is absolutely correct, you still have to convert it into Lean.

This is also why Peter Scholze, one of the greatest contemporary mathematicians, had grave doubts about his own proof before solving a major problem. He discussed it many times with his collaborators, and no one could say with certainty whether the result and proof process were correct. Even such a great and intelligent mathematician, who seems to have won a Fields Medal in 2018, could not say with certainty whether his own proof was correct. In the end, he found friends and collaborators, and they could only manually convert all the relevant mathematical theorems, definitions, lemmas, and so on into Lean. Then one day, once they had converted everything, Lean suddenly compiled successfully. That proved that the proof was correct: formal proof. Peter Scholze was extremely excited because it showed that the result was correct.

So even top scientists find it difficult to determine whether something is correct when handling highly complex mathematical problems. You can only trust logic and computers. Once the computer says it is correct, it must be correct. There is more than one such example. To prove whether something is correct, you must translate it into a logically derivable form that guarantees correctness.

items.question: Why do you think formalizing mathematical proofs in Lean takes so much time?
items.object: Formalizing mathematical proofs in Lean
items.answer: Because Lean is a structured language: you must convert all the relevant concepts in your mathematics, all the definitions you need, prior theorems, and so on, very rigorously according to its type language. That is, you must formalize every mathematical thing encountered throughout the entire derivation. So it takes a great deal of time.

items.question: How do you understand the role of inventing concepts in mathematics?
items.object: Mathematics as the invention of concepts and objects
items.answer: I think proof is certainly very important, but mathematics is, more importantly, a process of invention. Without concepts, there is no mathematics. The process of mathematical definition—the invention of mathematical objects and the process of defining mathematical objects—is indispensable for mathematics. At the very simplest level, beginning with the concept of number itself, you must first define number, then you can define addition and subtraction. Every mathematical definition uses mathematical concepts. What do integration and differentiation mean in calculus? What does an eigenvalue mean in linear algebra? What does a Riemannian metric mean in differential geometry? These are all concepts. The more important thing for a good mathematician is being able to find or define an extremely elegant mathematical concept or object—to abstract an essential mathematical definition. If you have an elegant and beautiful mathematical definition, that may be far more important than deriving the process itself. Without a suitable mathematical object, you cannot derive a mathematical process. If you study linear algebra and only see a pile of matrices, but cannot abstract from them a concept called an eigenvalue, then you cannot precisely capture the matrices’ internal structure. So the process of abstracting and defining a new object, a mathematical definition, from these mathematical objects is, I think, perhaps the most beautiful part of mathematics, or the part requiring the greatest insight.

items.question: Why do you think abstracting new concepts may be an insurmountable barrier for AI?
items.object: AI’s ability to abstract new concepts
items.answer: I do not think it can. It can never do it. I personally even think this part—the process of abstracting concepts—may not even be a computable process in the Turing sense. There may be some evidence for that. But having AI itself derive new concepts or abstract new concepts is an extremely difficult problem. Let alone in mathematics, where it would have to put forward new concepts among such complex relationships. Even with the most basic concept of number: imagine a language model that has never been trained on mathematics and does not know whether the concept of number exists. Like a primitive human: if a primitive person sees three geese, four birds, or five trees, that person can already begin to count and have the concept of number. They can define Arabic numerals and abstract the concept of number. The concept of number can be applied to any object, not necessarily birds; it can be used for anything. But if you only show AI these objects—three birds, four geese, and so on—it cannot extract the concept of number. I find it hard to imagine a program that, given such sensory input, can produce that concept. So I think the process of concept abstraction may be AGI’s final last mile, its final step. That mile may be forever impossible to cross. I think this process may not even be Turing-computable. This is also why I think the human brain, at its lowest level, may not be a Turing machine, may not be a process equivalent to a Turing machine.

items.question: Do you see mathematics as a human invention or as a structure inherent in the universe?
items.object: Mathematics as human invention or an inherent structure of the universe
items.answer: That is a huge question, and I think no matter what answer you give, it cannot be verified or falsified. You cannot have God tell you, “I made this universe using mathematics.” But this was the question mathematicians were discussing more than a century ago: what is the nature of mathematics? Is it invented or discovered? Did the universe itself originally contain the concept of number, or did people invent the concept of number? At the time there were several views: intuitionism, formalism, and logicism. What exactly is mathematics? Is it merely a formal system, a logical system, or an intuitive system created by humans? There is no conclusion, and perhaps there can never be one, even today. As I said earlier, this is not something that can be proved. But if I had to choose a side, I think mathematics is created by humans rather than numbers being inherent in the universe itself. As you just said, people saw two ducks, three geese, four chickens, abstracted the concept, and turned it into a language of expression through mathematical formulas. But the other part is that mathematics, as a logical system, is never self-consistent. There is a very famous theorem from the last century, perhaps one of the most important theorems in the history of mathematics, by Kurt Gödel: the incompleteness theorem. Any sufficiently powerful formal logical system always has some true facts that you cannot prove or verify. I do not believe the universe itself contains self-inconsistent parts. If the universe and mathematics correspond completely one-to-one, if human-created mathematics and a formal system correspond one-to-one, then there would be some self-inconsistent parts in the universe. I think that is difficult to understand, because the universe is a thing-in-itself. It is a thing that exists. It does not need to be described; it simply is what it is. Mathematics, as a logical system, has contradictions that can never be reconciled precisely because it is a human-made, invented logical system. Once something is human-made, it becomes troublesome, because it is not the ontology itself, not the thing-in-itself. It is a set of logic, symbols, and human-defined rules, so it will contain certain logical contradictions. This is only my personal view; it cannot be verified.

items.question: Why do you think automatic verification of a mathematical proof is insufficient to establish its value?
items.object: The value of automatically verified mathematical proofs
items.answer: I don’t think a result is necessarily enough simply because it is correct. Even if it has been automatically verified as correct, as humans we need to understand it and evaluate it. We have value judgments: does this verification and proof process have value? Does it contain insight? Perhaps an imperfect analogy would be this: if you want to attend a concert and hear a piano performance, and I tell you that the piano is played by a robot, and guarantee that the robot’s key pressure and duration are perfect, played according to the composer’s requirements, I would not want to listen.

That can resonate with you and move you. You know that a person spontaneously produced these things. I think this applies to science as well. items.question: How do you assess the value of scientific discoveries that humans cannot understand?
items.object: The value of scientific discoveries humans cannot understand
items.answer: I think they can only have partial meaning, instrumental meaning. If a discovery is useful as a tool—if its result is correct—then it has instrumental meaning. For example, in the 1970s, the four-color problem was proved: you can color the entire map with at most four colors. This was proved using mechanical computers in the 1970s. The result is certainly correct, but the proof process is tedious. It is essentially an enumeration process. From a practical perspective, the conclusion can be used to draw maps; you can use it, and it is certainly correct: you can draw maps using only four colors. But in terms of mathematics’ own value, it may not have especially great value, because it does not necessarily uncover a new theorem or particularly profound insight. So whether it has value depends entirely on whether it is useful, and on how you evaluate it and from which angle: do you evaluate it instrumentally, or in terms of value?

items.question: How do you see the difference between applying AI to physics and applying it to mathematics?
items.object: AI for Physics
items.answer: I think the biggest difference is that mathematics only exists in logical space. Mathematics is certainly part of physics, and many physical laws or derivations of new conclusions involve mathematics. But mathematics can live entirely in a logical space defined by humans, an ideal world. Physics must leave the logical world and enter the material world: you must verify it, you must run experiments. So AI for Physics may currently help solve certain physics problems—for example, solving partial differential equations, deriving new conclusions like Anthropic did earlier, and so on. That derives conclusions from a mathematical or formal-logical perspective. But if you want AI to develop new physical theories and validate them, it still has to go into the physical world. items.question: Why do you see abductive reasoning as such a difficult frontier for AI-driven scientific discovery?
items.object: Abductive reasoning in scientific discovery and AI
items.answer: Whether something is random is one matter, but once a random event occurs, you need to be able to discover the regularity behind it. This requires what is called abductive reasoning. Something happens to you—for example, an apple falls on my head. That is a random event. But humans can, like Newton, imagine what cause produced that random event. Using it as a trigger, he may develop an entire physical system. But what AI can currently do best among the full range of human reasoning patterns—deductive reasoning, inductive reasoning, and abductive reasoning, namely inferring possible causes from phenomena—is perhaps mainly deductive reasoning. Given premises, as in mathematics, I give you the theorems and definitions; can you derive a new conclusion? That is relatively easier to do logically. But with abductive reasoning, given a phenomenon, can you imagine a reasonable explanation and generalize that explanation to other phenomena? As with the earlier question, this involves abstraction, imagination, and a world model. These are all things AI currently cannot do, and I think it will not be able to do them even for a long time in the future. So indeed, any intellectual activity at an abstract level is, in my view, AGI’s final last mile.

items.question: How do you understand the value of apparently useless pursuits such as pure mathematics, art, and philosophy?
items.object: The value of apparently useless pursuits in mathematics, art, and philosophy
items.answer: I think whether mathematics, aesthetics, art, or philosophy, from a utility perspective these are all useless things. What use is a painting hanging in your home? No use at all. But without this supposedly useless effort—the great usefulness of uselessness—without these thought processes, aesthetic concepts, or mathematics derived purely from curiosity, pure spiritual enjoyment, you cannot derive physical processes. Perhaps the most beautiful things all begin with useless things; they begin with human curiosity, the curiosity of the mind, and the pursuit of beauty. Whether art, literature, or anything else, it is not useful at first. The same is true of philosophy. But useless does not mean it will not affect the future. During the whole process of thinking, it changes the state of your mind and how you understand the world. It is useful too; it is just that you cannot immediately perceive that usefulness. So generally speaking, any theoretical science—mathematics, especially pure mathematics, or art and philosophy in the humanities—belongs to what is called the great usefulness of uselessness.

items.question: How do you assess the practical potential of AI for mathematics to accelerate scientific progress today?
items.object: AI for mathematics as a tool for accelerating scientific progress
items.answer: I think AI for math can be used in many application contexts, whether solving equations in technological fields or—as with mathematics startups such as Axiom AI or Harmonic AI—using mathematical proof processes for chip verification or program verification. In any verification field, at this level there are already prospects for application and productization. In any computable domain, including when deriving new physical laws or equations, letting AI derive them can certainly be faster and more efficient than humans within a certain range. In these controllable environments, AI for math will certainly help scientific development as a whole. After all, much science needs to be mathematized. As long as you give it sufficient premises and conditions, and an appropriate context, it can put forward many new mathematical ideas. Even recently, Edward Witten—arguably the greatest contemporary theoretical physicist, the one who proposed string theory—published a paper on arXiv not long ago. He wrote, apparently in a footnote, that Claude helped him think of a section of that paper, or something along those lines. Even for new research results at Edward Witten’s level, at the most profound level, AI is already helping accelerate the process. So you can imagine that this phenomenon will only become more and more widespread in the future.

items.question: How do you assess AI’s ability to create new concepts?
items.object: AI’s ability to create new concepts
items.answer: It depends on how you define this concept. Concepts are very broad. There are very concrete concepts, like some of the specific things we may have mentioned earlier, which you can solve through clustering. If a representation can be mapped to—or what is called grounding—can be grounded in observations of the world, then I call that clustering. You see five chairs and might cluster them as chairs. When a sixth chair appears, because all of its features are roughly similar, you can recognize a similar cluster. That is already a concept. Any cluster, or a probabilistic manifold—a manifold—is a concept. This kind of thing has been doable for a long time. But the difficulty lies in abstract concepts such as those in creating mathematics. A concept can be applied in infinitely many situations, yet each of those situations has a stable similarity. I think these abstract concepts are very difficult, and may even be impossible to achieve with computational programs forever. So I see many, many levels, from the concrete to the abstract. Beyond a certain level, it becomes very difficult to achieve.

items.question: Why do you think people researching AI should read philosophy?
items.object: The relationship between philosophy, AI, and cognitive science
items.answer: I think many developments in AI today can be found reflected throughout the historical development of philosophy, because the questions philosophy explores—epistemology, for instance—are about how humans come to know the world. Starting with Plato and the so-called world of Forms: you have surely never seen a perfect circle in your life. Whether it is a tire or a plate, it is not perfect. But from these imperfect observations, you can arrive at a world of Forms—a perfect concept. This discussion has existed since very early on. It is really about how people generate knowledge and how they abstract these concepts. So you can look at it. The entire thread of philosophical development, the thread of AI development, and the thread of cognitive science development all address, in many ways, the same object. They simply use different languages and explore the question from different angles. But the object is the same: different mirrors reflecting the same thing.

items.question: Why do you think AI research needs more top-down thinking amid the current AI boom?
items.object: Top-down, first-principles thinking in AI research
items.answer:
I do think it does. AI is indeed extremely hot right now, perhaps the hottest topic in technology. Everyone wants to work on AI-related topics, make engineering improvements, think about how to apply it, and bring the technology into real-world use. Of course, that is a very important step in rolling out the technology. But most current applications, or so-called research, take a bottom-up perspective. Someone tells me that Transformers are useful and work well. The scaling law has not yet failed. You have to get the harness right. You have to build the infrastructure well. All of these things are things other people have told me. You make these capabilities work well and move upward, and then I can release the product. This is of course very important for short-term commercialization and putting AI into practice.

But beyond this rapidly changing research, I think there also needs to be research with loftier aspirations. If you really think from the top down, from first principles—what is intelligence? How do humans come to know the world? You need to think in reverse: what characteristics are there that current AI cannot achieve? If you reason backward in that way, you will find that AI cannot do many things, and that much more research is needed.

And this is not limited to AI. AI is computing; it is a computational program. The ultimate purpose of computing is to automate certain things. AI automates human thought processes—human intelligence. But intelligence is not the only thing computation can automate. It can automate physical processes, carry out modeling, automate processes, and so on. So from a more general perspective, from the perspective of computation, what can it ultimately accomplish? Beyond AI, if one day AI can approach the human level, what else can computation do? Once you think about that, there are still many very interesting topics.

I do think that amid the current AI frenzy, there are many interesting and important real-world implementations. But it will inevitably also produce a great deal of restlessness and some relatively superficial views. So top-down thinking is still needed.

items.question: How do you see the commercialization timeline for AI for Science?
items.object: Commercialization of AI for Science and science as a driver of AI development
items.answer: I think AI4S cannot be generalized about. AI4S already has room for real-world deployment, and there are already many deployed applications. Drug development, for example: even if in the end you are not yet able to sell an AI-generated drug, the various stages in the middle—the various targets, molecular structures, and so on—can already be commercialized as intermediate products. AI4S certainly has many levels, and some levels can already be brought to market. But if our goal is to achieve Nobel-level scientific results, then there is certainly still a long way to go. At that level, it is not AI4S—not treating science as an application on the assumption that AI is already strong enough—but rather AI and Science. That is, you not only have to do science, but before tackling such difficult problems, you need to improve AI's own capabilities. AI needs stronger abstraction capabilities, stronger reasoning capabilities, stronger abilities to conduct experiments and write code, and so on. If you cannot accomplish that, you cannot accomplish science at a higher level. This level will indeed be relatively long-term. It is not only a scientific problem; it is a fundamental AI research problem in itself. And I have always felt that science is not merely an application of AI. Rather, it should be a stimulus or catalyst that drives AI itself to develop better. If a model performs well on very difficult science problems, it should also be able to perform well on other problems—and better than current models—whether at the level of writing code or reasoning. Because if you can solve such hard problems, the model itself is already very strong. So it is not merely an application; as a driving force, it can develop better AI. Thus, commercialization paths are not a one-size-fits-all judgment, but layered. At some levels, commercialization is already possible for all these many labs and companies. But if you want to win a Nobel Prize, that will take a very long time.

items.question: Why do you think AI is still at least 20 or 30 years away from making autonomous Nobel Prize-level scientific discoveries?
items.object: AI making autonomous Nobel Prize-level scientific discoveries
items.answer: AlphaFold has already won one, but that was not an autonomous AI discovery. Still, if you want to win a Nobel Prize at this level, I think it will take at least 20 or 30 years. Plainly speaking, within the current AI paradigm, you would still need to strengthen capabilities it does not currently have. Leaving aside whether it can create entirely new concepts or abstract things out of thin air, if it can take the results of existing experiments and reason both forward and backward—this kind of causal reasoning, as mentioned earlier—that does not currently exist. How can it handle long-term memory? I have conducted countless experiments; how can I retrieve relevant memories from so many experiments? How can it continue learning continuously? By the time it can solve some of these current frontier topics, perhaps five or six years will already have passed. Then, if it goes on to conduct scientific experiments, it will certainly be stronger than today's AI. But at minimum, I think that will still take a great deal of time.

items.question: How do you see the broader significance for society of AI becoming capable of Nobel Prize–level scientific work?
items.object: AI for Science as a driver of broader AI capabilities
items.answer: I see AI as a meta technology, or a general-purpose technology. AI itself is a brain; you can add AI to anything. So it is not only AI plus science or technology; you can also say AI plus business. If you truly have something that intelligent, it certainly would not only solve scientific problems.
